sev0: Heel Pain in Children (Sever’s Disease): Symptoms, Treatment and Exercises | İhsan Eren
sev1: Does your child’s heel hurt after running and jumping? What is Sever’s disease, how long does it last, should they stop sport, and do heel cups help? Warning signs and three exercises to do at home.
sev3: Does your child say their heel hurts after running and jumping, or do they limp or walk on tiptoe? Irritation of the growth area of the heel bone during growth is called Sever’s disease. Despite its alarming name, it is a common, temporary condition linked to growth; the heel pain goes away once growth is complete.

sev11: Heel pain that gets worse with activities such as running and jumping and eases with rest.
sev13: Tenderness when the heel is squeezed from both sides; mild swelling where the Achilles tendon attaches to the bone.
sev14: Tight calf muscles; in one or both heels.
sev15: During growth spurts, the bones grow faster than the calf muscles and the Achilles tendon.
sev16: The tight Achilles tendon pulls repeatedly on the growth area of the heel bone and irritates it.
sev17: This is why it can come back with each new growth spurt.
sev19: If the pain is severe, take a break from running and jumping; swimming and cycling are good options. Rest with the leg raised after sport.
sev21: You can put ice wrapped in a towel on the heel for 10–15 minutes, especially after activity.
sev23: Use shock-absorbing insoles or gel heel cups and supportive shoes; avoid walking around barefoot.
sev25: Calf stretches reduce tightness. If the pain returns during a new growth spurt, start the stretches again.
sev26: Three exercises to relax the calves
sev27: Do the stretches slowly and without forcing. If an exercise makes the pain worse or causes new pain, stop and ask a specialist.
sev28: Calf stretch with a straight knee
sev29: Stand facing a wall with your hands on it. Keep one leg behind you with the knee straight; press the back heel into the floor and lean forwards until you feel a stretch in your calf.
sev32: Stand with one foot in front of the other and both heels on the floor. Bend both knees slightly; you will feel the stretch in the lower calf, near the heel.
sev34: Sit or lie down. Pull your foot up towards you and hold for 5 seconds, then point your toes towards the floor and hold for 5 seconds.
sev36: They don’t need to stop completely. If the pain is severe, they can take a break from sports involving running and jumping until it settles; in the meantime, lower-impact activities such as swimming and cycling are a good choice. Once the pain has gone, they can build their activity back up gradually.
sev37: The heel pain usually goes away once growth is complete. It can come back several times during periods of growth. If there is no improvement within 6 weeks despite following the advice, you can see a specialist.
sev38: Do heel cups or insoles help?
sev39: Small studies found that gel heel cups and shock-absorbing insoles reduced pain in the short term. In a study of 124 children, all groups improved markedly within 2 months; the extra difference from heel cups was small, and changing footwear made no extra difference.
sev41: In a study of 101 children, there was no difference at 3 months between waiting and watching, shock-absorbing heel cups, and physiotherapy with calf strengthening. So most children get better with simple measures. If the pain does not go away or keeps coming back, a personalised assessment can help guide you.
sev42: Why do both heels sometimes hurt at once?
sev43: Because the condition is linked to growth, it can affect one heel or both at the same time.
